paragraphs.text: וַיֵּ֣שֶׁב יַעֲקֹ֔ב בְּאֶ֖רֶץ מְגוּרֵ֣י אָבִ֑יו בְּאֶ֖רֶץ כְּנָֽעַן׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov dwelt in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Kena'an.

paragraphs.text: אֵ֣לֶּה ׀ תֹּלְד֣וֹת יַעֲקֹ֗ב יוֹסֵ֞ף בֶּן־שְׁבַֽע־עֶשְׂרֵ֤ה שָׁנָה֙ הָיָ֨ה רֹעֶ֤ה אֶת־אֶחָיו֙ בַּצֹּ֔אן וְה֣וּא נַ֗עַר אֶת־בְּנֵ֥י בִלְהָ֛ה וְאֶת־בְּנֵ֥י זִלְפָּ֖ה נְשֵׁ֣י אָבִ֑יו וַיָּבֵ֥א יוֹסֵ֛ף אֶת־דִּבָּתָ֥ם רָעָ֖ה אֶל־אֲבִיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: These are the generations of Ya'aqov. Yosef, being seventeen years old, was feeding the flock with his brethren; and he was a lad with the sons of Bilhah, and with the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives: and Yosef brought their evil report to their father.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Elleh toledot Ya'aqov* — *these are the* toledot *of Ya'aqov* — is the last of the ten *toledot*-formulae that structure Genesis, but it heads a **narrative cycle** (the Yosef story, Gen 37-50) rather than a genealogy, and names the father while the section is about the sons. The WoH translation renders the ASV-baseline 'And these are the generations of Ya'aqov', consistent with the chapter-25 and chapter-36 *toledot*-header convention; the narrative-sensitive alternatives ('this is the story / the line of Ya'aqov', NJPS; 'the lineage', Alter; and the central glossary `toledot` entry's 'tale of') are noted but not adopted, for corpus-wide header consistency. See the overlay entry `toledot-yaaqov-narrative-cycle-header`.

*Ve-hu na'ar* — 'and he was a *na'ar*'. נַעַר spans 'youth/lad' (descriptive of age) and 'servant-lad / attendant' (a subordinate in service). The *et* before *benei Vilhah* most naturally marks an object, supporting the attendant-reading: Yosef served as a junior attendant *to* the sons of the handmaid-wives (NJPS 'a helper to the sons'), which sharpens the brothers' resentment. The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline 'a lad with the sons of Bilhah... and Zilpah', preserving the ambiguity. See `naar-lad-youth-or-attendant`.

*Dibbatam ra'ah* — 'their evil report'. דִּבָּה carries a negative core ('whispering, slander, ill report'), so *ra'ah* ('evil') is nearly pleonastic, and the phrase is doubly ambiguous: a report *about* the brothers' misconduct, or a *malicious / slanderous* report (Yosef as tale-bearer); and the text leaves unstated whether what he reported was true. The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline 'their evil report', preserving the ambiguity. See `dibbatam-raah-evil-report-slander`.

paragraphs.text: וְיִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אָהַ֤ב אֶת־יוֹסֵף֙ מִכָּל־בָּנָ֔יו כִּֽי־בֶן־זְקֻנִ֥ים ה֖וּא ל֑וֹ וְעָ֥שָׂה ל֖וֹ כְּתֹ֥נֶת פַּסִּֽים׃

i18n.en: Now Yisra'el loved Yosef more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Ki ven-zequnim hu lo* — 'because he was the son of his old age'. The idiom *ben-zequnim* marks Yosef as Ya'aqov's cherished late-born (cf. Yitzchaq, Gen 21:2 + 7; Binyamin, Gen 44:20); Targum Onqelos reads it instead as 'a wise son' (*bar chakkim*), via the elder-as-sage association. The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline plain-sense rendering. See `ben-zequnim-son-of-old-age`.

*Ketonet passim* — the chapter's largest philological crux (recurs vv 23, 32). The phrase occurs only here and at 2 Sam 13:18-19 (of Tamar's royal-virgin garment), which is decisive: three readings compete — (a) 'of many colours' (LXX χιτὼν ποικίλος, Vulgate *polymita*, KJV/ASV — venerable but with no clear derivation from *pas*); (b) 'reaching to the palms and soles' / long-sleeved (b. Shabbat 10b, Ibn Ezra; *pas* = palm/sole, cf. Dan 5:5 *pas yeda*; the 2 Sam 13 parallel supports a full-length status-robe); (c) 'an ornamented / fine tunic' (NJPS, Speiser, connecting Akkadian *kitû pišannu*). The modern critical consensus has moved away from 'colours' toward a **status-marking** rather than colour-marking garment (a long-sleeved, ankle-length robe impractical for labour, marking the wearer as set apart). The WoH translation retains the ASV-baseline 'a coat of many colours' on the surface per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention, while flagging here that the philologically stronger readings are the long-sleeved / ornamented status-tunic. See the central glossary entry `ketonet-passim-ornamented-tunic-crux`.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּרְא֣וּ אֶחָ֗יו כִּֽי־אֹת֞וֹ אָהַ֤ב אֲבִיהֶם֙ מִכָּל־אֶחָ֔יו וַֽיִּשְׂנְא֖וּ אֹת֑וֹ וְלֹ֥א יָכְל֖וּ דַּבְּר֥וֹ לְשָׁלֹֽם׃

i18n.en: And his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren; and they hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּחֲלֹ֤ם יוֹסֵף֙ חֲל֔וֹם וַיַּגֵּ֖ד לְאֶחָ֑יו וַיּוֹסִ֥פוּ ע֖וֹד שְׂנֹ֥א אֹתֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Yosef dreamed a dream, and he told it to his brethren: and they hated him yet the more.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֖אמֶר אֲלֵיהֶ֑ם שִׁמְעוּ־נָ֕א הַחֲל֥וֹם הַזֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר חָלָֽמְתִּי׃

i18n.en: And he said to them, Hear, I pray you, this dream which I have dreamed:

paragraphs.text: וְ֠הִנֵּה אֲנַ֜חְנוּ מְאַלְּמִ֤ים אֲלֻמִּים֙ בְּת֣וֹךְ הַשָּׂדֶ֔ה וְהִנֵּ֛ה קָ֥מָה אֲלֻמָּתִ֖י וְגַם־נִצָּ֑בָה וְהִנֵּ֤ה תְסֻבֶּ֙ינָה֙ אֲלֻמֹּ֣תֵיכֶ֔ם וַתִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֖יןָ לַאֲלֻמָּתִֽי׃

i18n.en: for, behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and, lo, my sheaf arose, and also stood upright; and, behold, your sheaves came round about, and made obeisance to my sheaf.

paragraphs.commentary: *Va-tishtachaveynah la-alumati* — 'made obeisance to my sheaf'. The Hishtaphel of חוה (the *yštḥwy* stem, cf. Ugaritic) denotes full prostration / homage before a superior — the same verb used for worship. It is the structural keyword of the Yosef cycle: the sheaves (v 7), then the sun, moon, and eleven stars (v 9), then Ya'aqov's own family in his incredulous question (v 10) 'make obeisance', foreshadowing the brothers' literal prostration before Yosef in Mitsrayim (Gen 42:6; 43:26 + 28; 44:14; 50:18). The WoH translation renders the ASV-baseline 'made obeisance' consistently at vv 7, 9, 10. See `hishtachavah-bow-down-obeisance-worship` (the central glossary entry covering the dream-and-fulfilment arc).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמְרוּ לוֹ֙ אֶחָ֔יו הֲמָלֹ֤ךְ תִּמְלֹךְ֙ עָלֵ֔ינוּ אִם־מָשׁ֥וֹל תִּמְשֹׁ֖ל בָּ֑נוּ וַיּוֹסִ֤פוּ עוֹד֙ שְׂנֹ֣א אֹת֔וֹ עַל־חֲלֹמֹתָ֖יו וְעַל־דְּבָרָֽיו׃

i18n.en: And his brethren said to him, Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us? And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּחֲלֹ֥ם עוֹד֙ חֲל֣וֹם אַחֵ֔ר וַיְסַפֵּ֥ר אֹת֖וֹ לְאֶחָ֑יו וַיֹּ֗אמֶר הִנֵּ֨ה חָלַ֤מְתִּֽי חֲלוֹם֙ ע֔וֹד וְהִנֵּ֧ה הַשֶּׁ֣מֶשׁ וְהַיָּרֵ֗חַ וְאַחַ֤ד עָשָׂר֙ כּֽוֹכָבִ֔ים מִֽשְׁתַּחֲוִ֖ים לִֽי׃

i18n.en: And he dreamed yet another dream, and told it to his brethren, and said, Behold, I have dreamed yet a dream; and, behold, the sun and the moon and eleven stars made obeisance to me.

paragraphs.commentary: The second dream — *ha-shemesh ve-ha-yareach ve-achad asar kokhavim mishtachavim li*, 'the sun and the moon and eleven stars made obeisance to me' — uses the same obeisance-verb as v 7 (see the v 7 note and `hishtachavah-bow-down-obeisance-worship`). The eleven stars are the eleven other brothers; the sun and moon are read by Ya'aqov as himself and (v 10) Yosef's mother — a celestial-family image whose astral idiom is widely paralleled in ANE dream-and-omen literature.

paragraphs.text: וַיְסַפֵּ֣ר אֶל־אָבִיו֮ וְאֶל־אֶחָיו֒ וַיִּגְעַר־בּ֣וֹ אָבִ֔יו וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֔וֹ מָ֛ה הַחֲל֥וֹם הַזֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁ֣ר חָלָ֑מְתָּ הֲב֣וֹא נָב֗וֹא אֲנִי֙ וְאִמְּךָ֣ וְאַחֶ֔יךָ לְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֺ֥ת לְךָ֖ אָֽרְצָה׃

i18n.en: And he told it to his father, and to his brethren; and his father rebuked him, and said to him, What is this dream that thou hast dreamed? Shall I and thy mother and thy brethren indeed come to bow down ourselves to thee to the earth?

paragraphs.commentary: *Le-hishtachavot lekha artzah* — 'to bow down to thee to the earth'. Ya'aqov's rebuke uses the same obeisance-verb (v 7, v 9; see `hishtachavah-bow-down-obeisance-worship`), here with *artzah* ('to the earth/ground') making the prostration explicit. The mention of 'thy mother' bowing is itself a crux (Rachel is dead, Gen 35:19), variously read as referring to Bilhah, Le'ah, or as a feature of the dream's schematic completeness; the translation renders the surface plainly.

paragraphs.text: וַיְקַנְאוּ־ב֖וֹ אֶחָ֑יו וְאָבִ֖יו שָׁמַ֥ר אֶת־הַדָּבָֽר׃

i18n.en: And his brethren envied him; but his father kept the saying in mind.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ אֶחָ֑יו לִרְע֛וֹת אֶׄתׄ־צֹ֥אן אֲבִיהֶ֖ם בִּשְׁכֶֽם׃

i18n.en: And his brethren went to feed their father's flock in Shechem.

paragraphs.commentary: The Masoretic text marks **puncta extraordinaria** (supralinear scribal dots, נקודות) over אֶׄתׄ — the *nota accusativa* (direct-object marker) before *tzon* ('flock'). These scribal dots, one of the fifteen sets of *puncta extraordinaria* in the HB, flag a textual/exegetical note on the particle (the rabbinic tradition variously took the dots to question whether the brothers went to tend the *flock* or, euphemistically, to tend *themselves*). The translation surface is unaffected ('their father's flock'); the marking is recorded here per the principle of preserving the source's scribal apparatus, cross-referenced to the Gen 18:9 and Gen 33:4 *puncta* already governed by the central entry `puncta-extraordinaria-v9-elav` (whose *appliesTo* is extended to GEN-WOH-37:12 in this pass).

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל אֶל־יוֹסֵ֗ף הֲל֤וֹא אַחֶ֙יךָ֙ רֹעִ֣ים בִּשְׁכֶ֔ם לְכָ֖ה וְאֶשְׁלָחֲךָ֣ אֲלֵיהֶ֑ם וַיֹּ֥אמֶר ל֖וֹ הִנֵּֽנִי׃

i18n.en: And Yisra'el said to Yosef, Are not thy brethren feeding the flock in Shechem? come, and I will send thee to them. And he said to him, Here am I.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ לֶךְ־נָ֨א רְאֵ֜ה אֶת־שְׁל֤וֹם אַחֶ֙יךָ֙ וְאֶת־שְׁל֣וֹם הַצֹּ֔אן וַהֲשִׁבֵ֖נִי דָּבָ֑ר וַיִּשְׁלָחֵ֙הוּ֙ מֵעֵ֣מֶק חֶבְר֔וֹן וַיָּבֹ֖א שְׁכֶֽמָה׃

i18n.en: And he said to him, Go now, see whether it is well with thy brethren, and well with the flock; and bring me word again. So he sent him out of the vale of Hevron, and he came to Shechem.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּמְצָאֵ֣הוּ אִ֔ישׁ וְהִנֵּ֥ה תֹעֶ֖ה בַּשָּׂדֶ֑ה וַיִּשְׁאָלֵ֧הוּ הָאִ֛ישׁ לֵאמֹ֖ר מַה־תְּבַקֵּֽשׁ׃

i18n.en: And a certain man found him, and, behold, he was wandering in the field: and the man asked him, saying, What seekest thou?

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֕אמֶר אֶת־אַחַ֖י אָנֹכִ֣י מְבַקֵּ֑שׁ הַגִּֽידָה־נָּ֣א לִ֔י אֵיפֹ֖ה הֵ֥ם רֹעִֽים׃

i18n.en: And he said, I am seeking my brethren: tell me, I pray thee, where they are feeding the flock.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָאִישׁ֙ נָסְע֣וּ מִזֶּ֔ה כִּ֤י שָׁמַ֙עְתִּי֙ אֹֽמְרִ֔ים נֵלְכָ֖ה דֹּתָ֑יְנָה וַיֵּ֤לֶךְ יוֹסֵף֙ אַחַ֣ר אֶחָ֔יו וַיִּמְצָאֵ֖ם בְּדֹתָֽן׃

i18n.en: And the man said, They are departed from here; for I heard them say, Let us go to Dotan. And Yosef went after his brethren, and found them in Dotan.

paragraphs.commentary: The toponym appears in two forms: the directional/locative דֹּתָיְנָה (*Dotaynah*, 'to/toward Dotan', v 17a) and the bare דֹּתָן (*Dotan*, v 17b). The WoH translation collapses the locative to the base form and carries the directional sense with the English preposition ('Let us go to Dotan'; 'found them in Dotan'), consistent with the v 14 Shechemah → Shechem treatment, and uses the WoH 't'-transliteration ('Dotan', not the ASV/KJV 'Dothan'). Dotan is identified with Tell Dothan, ca. 22 km north of Shechem on the trunk-road toward Egypt (cf. 2 Kgs 6:13). See `dotan-toponym-locative-form`.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּרְא֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ מֵרָחֹ֑ק וּבְטֶ֙רֶם֙ יִקְרַ֣ב אֲלֵיהֶ֔ם וַיִּֽתְנַכְּל֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ לַהֲמִיתֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And they saw him afar off, and before he came near to them, they conspired against him to slay him.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֖וּ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־אָחִ֑יו הִנֵּ֗ה בַּ֛עַל הַחֲלֹמ֥וֹת הַלָּזֶ֖ה בָּֽא׃

i18n.en: And they said one to another, Behold, this dreamer cometh.

paragraphs.commentary: *Hinneh ba'al ha-chalomot ha-lazeh ba* — 'behold, this dreamer cometh'. *Ba'al ha-chalomot* is literally 'lord/master/owner of *the* dreams' — a sarcastic mock-title (Alter 'here comes that dream-master'). The taunt's bite is the irony: the brothers, who have just refused Yosef's dream that he would *rule* over them (v 8), mock him with a mock-honorific ('lord of dreams') that ironically concedes the very lordship-claim they reject. The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline idiomatic 'this dreamer'; the literal *ba'al*-sarcasm is documented in `baal-ha-chalomot-dream-master-epithet`.

paragraphs.text: וְעַתָּ֣ה ׀ לְכ֣וּ וְנַֽהַרְגֵ֗הוּ וְנַשְׁלִכֵ֙הוּ֙ בְּאַחַ֣ד הַבֹּר֔וֹת וְאָמַ֕רְנוּ חַיָּ֥ה רָעָ֖ה אֲכָלָ֑תְהוּ וְנִרְאֶ֕ה מַה־יִּהְי֖וּ חֲלֹמֹתָֽיו׃

i18n.en: Come now therefore, and let us slay him, and cast him into one of the pits, and we will say, An evil beast hath devoured him: and we shall see what will become of his dreams.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Chayah ra'ah akhalat-hu* — 'an evil beast hath devoured him' — the cover-story the brothers invent (and which Ya'aqov repeats at v 33). *Chayah ra'ah* is ambiguous between 'an *evil* beast' (ASV/KJV — but *ra'ah* applied to an animal does not mean morally wicked) and the philologically natural 'a *wild / savage / ferocious* beast' (NJPS 'a savage beast'; NRSV 'a wild animal'). The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline 'an evil beast' at vv 20 and 33; see `chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast`.

*Bor* — 'pit'. The word denotes specifically a rock-cut water-cistern (a bottle-shaped, smooth-walled, plastered shaft), as v 24's gloss makes explicit ('the bor was empty, no water in it'): a *dry* cistern, deep enough that Yosef must be 'drawn up' (v 28). The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline 'pit' at vv 20, 22, 24, 28, 29 (which also preserves the resonance with the poetic 'pit' of descent activated by the She'ol-motif at v 35); the cistern-specificity is documented in the central glossary entry `bor-pit-cistern-dry-water-shaft`.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּשְׁמַ֣ע רְאוּבֵ֔ן וַיַּצִּלֵ֖הוּ מִיָּדָ֑ם וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לֹ֥א נַכֶּ֖נּוּ נָֽפֶשׁ׃

i18n.en: And Re'uven heard it, and delivered him out of their hand, and said, Let us not take his life.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֲלֵהֶ֣ם ׀ רְאוּבֵן֮ אַל־תִּשְׁפְּכוּ־דָם֒ הַשְׁלִ֣יכוּ אֹת֗וֹ אֶל־הַבּ֤וֹר הַזֶּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּמִּדְבָּ֔ר וְיָ֖ד אַל־תִּשְׁלְחוּ־ב֑וֹ לְמַ֗עַן הַצִּ֤יל אֹתוֹ֙ מִיָּדָ֔ם לַהֲשִׁיב֖וֹ אֶל־אָבִֽיו׃

i18n.en: And Re'uven said to them, Shed no blood; cast him into this pit that is in the wilderness, but lay no hand upon him: that he might deliver him out of their hand, to restore him to his father.

paragraphs.commentary: Re’uven’s counsel — *al-tishpekhu dam... hashlikhu oto el ha-bor* ("shed no blood; cast him into this pit") — names the same dry cistern as v 20 (see that note and `bor-pit-cistern-dry-water-shaft`); his aim, the narrator discloses, was to deliver Yosef and restore him to his father.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֕י כַּֽאֲשֶׁר־בָּ֥א יוֹסֵ֖ף אֶל־אֶחָ֑יו וַיַּפְשִׁ֤יטוּ אֶת־יוֹסֵף֙ אֶת־כֻּתָּנְתּ֔וֹ אֶת־כְּתֹ֥נֶת הַפַּסִּ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָלָֽיו׃

i18n.en: And it came to pass, when Yosef was come to his brethren, that they stripped Yosef of his coat, the coat of many colours that was on him;

paragraphs.commentary: *Et-ketonto et-ketonet ha-passim asher alav* — they strip Yosef of "his coat, the coat of many colours." The doubled designation (the generic *ketonet* then the specific *ketonet ha-passim*) underscores the garment that is the engine of the plot; on the *passim* crux see the v 3 note and `ketonet-passim-ornamented-tunic-crux`.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּ֨קָּחֻ֔הוּ וַיַּשְׁלִ֥כוּ אֹת֖וֹ הַבֹּ֑רָה וְהַבּ֣וֹר רֵ֔ק אֵ֥ין בּ֖וֹ מָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: and they took him, and cast him into the pit: and the pit was empty, there was no water in it.

paragraphs.commentary: *Ve-ha-bor req ein bo mayim* — 'and the pit was empty, there was no water in it'. The narrator's gloss tells the reader the *bor* (v 20 note) is a **dry** cistern — which is why Yosef can be cast in and survive, and why the brothers can sit beside it to eat (v 25). The directional form *ha-borah* ('into the pit') uses the locative he. See `bor-pit-cistern-dry-water-shaft`.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּשְׁבוּ֮ לֶֽאֱכָל־לֶחֶם֒ וַיִּשְׂא֤וּ עֵֽינֵיהֶם֙ וַיִּרְא֔וּ וְהִנֵּה֙ אֹרְחַ֣ת יִשְׁמְעֵאלִ֔ים בָּאָ֖ה מִגִּלְעָ֑ד וּגְמַלֵּיהֶ֣ם נֹֽשְׂאִ֗ים נְכֹאת֙ וּצְרִ֣י וָלֹ֔ט הוֹלְכִ֖ים לְהוֹרִ֥יד מִצְרָֽיְמָה׃

i18n.en: And they sat down to eat bread: and they lifted up their eyes and looked, and, behold, a caravan of Yishme'elim was coming from Gil'ad, with their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going to carry it down to Mitsrayim.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Orchat Yishme'elim* — 'a caravan of Yishme'elim'. This verse opens the chapter's classic **documentary doublet**: here a caravan of *Ishmaelites* approaches from Gil'ad; v 27 has Yehudah propose selling to the *Ishmaelites*; v 28 has *Midianites* draw Yosef from the pit and sell him to the *Ishmaelites*; v 36 has the *Medanites* sell him in Mitsrayim. On the standard source-critical reading two sale-traditions are interwoven (J: Yehudah / Ishmaelites; E: Re'uven / Midianites); the harmonizing tradition reads the groups as overlapping nomad confederations (decisively, Judg 8:24 glosses defeated *Midianites* as *'for they were Ishmaelites'*, and Ishmael, Midian, and Medan are all Abrahamic, Gen 25:1-4). The WoH translation preserves all three ethnonyms verbatim (transliterated -im plurals) and does not smooth the seam, documenting both readings as named scholarly positions. See `ishmaelite-midianite-medanite-documentary-doublet` (sibling-overlay treatment per the ratified Gen-35 pattern; flagged as a promotion candidate pending a Judges translation).

The cargo *nekhot u-tzeri va-lot* — ASV 'spicery, balm, and myrrh' — is a convoy of aromatics down the incense-route: *nekhot* (gum / tragacanth), *tzeri* (the balm of Gil'ad, cf. Jer 8:22), and *lot* (more precisely ladanum / labdanum, the rock-rose resin, not true myrrh). The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline renderings; the modern botanical identifications are documented in `nekhot-tzeri-lot-caravan-spices`. (The lift-the-eyes idiom *va-yis'u eineihem* is governed by the central `sa-eynekha-lift-your-eyes` entry, already referenced.)

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יְהוּדָ֖ה אֶל־אֶחָ֑יו מַה־בֶּ֗צַע כִּ֤י נַהֲרֹג֙ אֶת־אָחִ֔ינוּ וְכִסִּ֖ינוּ אֶת־דָּמֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: And Yehudah said to his brethren, What profit is it if we slay our brother and conceal his blood?

paragraphs.text: לְכ֞וּ וְנִמְכְּרֶ֣נּוּ לַיִּשְׁמְעֵאלִ֗ים וְיָדֵ֙נוּ֙ אַל־תְּהִי־ב֔וֹ כִּֽי־אָחִ֥ינוּ בְשָׂרֵ֖נוּ ה֑וּא וַֽיִּשְׁמְע֖וּ אֶחָֽיו׃

i18n.en: Come, and let us sell him to the Yishme'elim, and let not our hand be upon him; for he is our brother, our flesh. And his brethren hearkened to him.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּֽעַבְרוּ֩ אֲנָשִׁ֨ים מִדְיָנִ֜ים סֹֽחֲרִ֗ים וַֽיִּמְשְׁכוּ֙ וַיַּֽעֲל֤וּ אֶת־יוֹסֵף֙ מִן־הַבּ֔וֹר וַיִּמְכְּר֧וּ אֶת־יוֹסֵ֛ף לַיִּשְׁמְעֵאלִ֖ים בְּעֶשְׂרִ֣ים כָּ֑סֶף וַיָּבִ֥יאוּ אֶת־יוֹסֵ֖ף מִצְרָֽיְמָה׃

i18n.en: And there passed by Midyanim, merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Yosef out of the pit, and sold Yosef to the Yishme'elim for twenty pieces of silver. And they brought Yosef into Mitsrayim.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Anashim Midyanim socharim* — 'Midyanim, merchantmen'. The grammatical subject of *va-yimsh'khu va-ya'alu* ('they drew and lifted up') is ambiguous — the brothers, or the passing Midyanim — and 'sold Yosef to the Yishme'elim' compounds the tension of the three-ethnonym doublet (see the v 25 note and `ishmaelite-midianite-medanite-documentary-doublet`). The WoH translation preserves the MT as it stands.

*Be-esrim kasef* — 'for twenty pieces of silver'. The unit-word *kasef* ('silver') stands without an explicit denomination; the implied unit is the shekel, and twenty shekels is the age-and-period-appropriate price of a young male slave (cf. Lev 27:5; Exod 21:32's thirty shekels; the Code of Hammurabi and Nuzi/Mari slave-prices). The existing central money-unit entries (`kesitah`, the Gen 23 *kesef* formulae, the Gen 24 weight-units) do **not** govern this sale-price; see the dedicated overlay entry `twenty-kesef-slave-price-yosef-sale`.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֤שָׁב רְאוּבֵן֙ אֶל־הַבּ֔וֹר וְהִנֵּ֥ה אֵין־יוֹסֵ֖ף בַּבּ֑וֹר וַיִּקְרַ֖ע אֶת־בְּגָדָֽיו׃

i18n.en: And Re'uven returned to the pit; and, behold, Yosef was not in the pit; and he rent his clothes.

paragraphs.commentary: Re’uven returns to the *bor* (v 20 note; `bor-pit-cistern-dry-water-shaft`) to find it empty and rends his clothes — his rescue-plan (v 22) undone, unaware of the sale transacted in his absence.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֥שָׁב אֶל־אֶחָ֖יו וַיֹּאמַ֑ר הַיֶּ֣לֶד אֵינֶ֔נּוּ וַאֲנִ֖י אָ֥נָה אֲנִי־בָֽא׃

i18n.en: And he returned to his brethren, and said, The child is not; and I, where shall I go?

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְח֖וּ אֶת־כְּתֹ֣נֶת יוֹסֵ֑ף וַֽיִּשְׁחֲטוּ֙ שְׂעִ֣יר עִזִּ֔ים וַיִּטְבְּל֥וּ אֶת־הַכֻּתֹּ֖נֶת בַּדָּֽם׃

i18n.en: And they took Yosef's coat, and killed a he-goat, and dipped the coat in the blood;

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְשַׁלְּח֞וּ אֶת־כְּתֹ֣נֶת הַפַּסִּ֗ים וַיָּבִ֙יאוּ֙ אֶל־אֲבִיהֶ֔ם וַיֹּאמְר֖וּ זֹ֣את מָצָ֑אנוּ הַכֶּר־נָ֗א הַכְּתֹ֧נֶת בִּנְךָ֛ הִ֖וא אִם־לֹֽא׃

i18n.en: and they sent the coat of many colours, and they brought it to their father, and said, This have we found: know now whether it is thy son's coat or not.

paragraphs.commentary: *Haker-na ha-ketonet binkha hi im-lo* — 'know now whether it is thy son's coat or not'. The verb is the Hiphil of נכר ('recognise / identify'), answered in v 33 by *va-yakkirah* ('and he recognised it') — a deliberate recognition-loop that 'know now' (ASV) flattens. The *haker-na... va-yakkirah* pairing is a structural echo: Ya'aqov, who once deceived his blind father by *defeating* recognition (Gen 27:23, with a goat — *se'ir izzim*, cf. v 31 here), is now deceived by his sons *through* recognition (a goat's blood on the tunic) — measure for measure; and the identical formula *haker-na* returns in the very next chapter when Tamar confronts Yehudah (Gen 38:25-26), binding the engineer of this deception to his own. The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline 'know now'; the *nakar*-recognition force and the cross-chapter motif are documented in `haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif`. The garment is again the *ketonet passim* (v 3 note).

paragraphs.text: וַיַּכִּירָ֤הּ וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ כְּתֹ֣נֶת בְּנִ֔י חַיָּ֥ה רָעָ֖ה אֲכָלָ֑תְהוּ טָרֹ֥ף טֹרַ֖ף יוֹסֵֽף׃

i18n.en: And he knew it, and said, It is my son's coat; an evil beast hath devoured him; Yosef is without doubt torn in pieces.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Chayah ra'ah akhalat-hu* — Ya'aqov, deceived, repeats the brothers' invented cover-story (v 20 note; `chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast`).

*Tarof toraf Yosef* — 'Yosef is without doubt torn in pieces'. The construction is the emphatic infinitive-absolute + finite verb (*tarof toraf*) of the root טרף ('to tear / rend [by a wild beast]'), an intensive 'surely / utterly torn' — the same doubled-infinitive intensive pattern governed across the corpus by the central entry `harbah-arbeh-doubled-infinitive-intensive` (cf. *mot tamut*, Gen 2:17). The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline 'without doubt torn in pieces', which captures the intensive; the doubled-infinitive force is carried in the apparatus per the standing pattern.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרַ֤ע יַעֲקֹב֙ שִׂמְלֹתָ֔יו וַיָּ֥שֶׂם שַׂ֖ק בְּמָתְנָ֑יו וַיִּתְאַבֵּ֥ל עַל־בְּנ֖וֹ יָמִ֥ים רַבִּֽים׃

i18n.en: And Ya'aqov rent his garments, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days.

paragraphs.commentary: *Va-yasem saq be-motnav* — 'and put sackcloth upon his loins'. שַׂק (*saq*) is the coarse haircloth mourning-garment, worn against the skin at the waist as the standard gesture of grief and lament (cf. Job 16:15; 2 Sam 3:31; Jon 3:5-6; Est 4:1) — the first weighty occurrence in Genesis. The standard rendering 'sackcloth' (ASV/KJV/NJPS) is uncontested and is retained without a glossary entry; the term is noted here for its cultic/mourning weight across the HB.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּקֻמוּ֩ כָל־בָּנָ֨יו וְכָל־בְּנֹתָ֜יו לְנַחֲמ֗וֹ וַיְמָאֵן֙ לְהִתְנַחֵ֔ם וַיֹּ֕אמֶר כִּֽי־אֵרֵ֧ד אֶל־בְּנִ֛י אָבֵ֖ל שְׁאֹ֑לָה וַיֵּ֥בְךְּ אֹת֖וֹ אָבִֽיו׃

i18n.en: And all his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him; but he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down to She'ol to my son mourning. And his father wept for him.

paragraphs.commentary: *Ki ered el-beni avel She'olah* — 'For I will go down to She'ol to my son mourning'. This is the first weighty occurrence of שְׁאוֹל in the Yosef cycle and the chapter's principal theological-lexical decision. *She'ol* names the ancient-Hebrew realm of the dead — a subterranean abode to which all the dead descend (hence *ered... She'olah*, 'I will go *down* to She'ol'); it is neither the individual tomb (*qever*) nor the later Christian 'hell'. The KJV/ASV tradition renders 'the grave', flattening the cosmological register; the modern critical tradition (NJPS, NRSV, Alter) transliterates 'Sheol'. The WoH translation transliterates **She'ol** per the corpus loaded-term convention, documenting the underworld / grave / realm-of-the-dead semantic range without importing any cosmological synthesis beyond the mainstream ANE picture. Ya'aqov's vow to descend *mourning* to She'ol recurs in the cycle (Gen 42:38; 44:29 + 31). See the central glossary entry `sheol-underworld-realm-of-the-dead`.

paragraphs.text: וְהַ֨מְּדָנִ֔ים מָכְר֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ אֶל־מִצְרָ֑יִם לְפֽוֹטִיפַר֙ סְרִ֣יס פַּרְעֹ֔ה שַׂ֖ר הַטַּבָּחִֽים׃ (פ)

i18n.en: And the Medanim sold him into Mitsrayim to Potifar, an officer of Pharaoh's, the captain of the guard.

paragraphs.commentary:
*Ha-Medanim* — 'the Medanim'. The MT reads מְדָנִים (Medanites), a third gentilic distinct from the מִדְיָנִים (Midyanim) of v 28; the LXX and Samaritan Pentateuch harmonize to *Midianitai*. The WoH translation preserves the MT *Medanim* (transliterated) as the principal reading, part of the chapter's three-ethnonym documentary tension (see the v 25 note and `ishmaelite-midianite-medanite-documentary-doublet`).

*Seris Par'oh* — 'an officer of Pharaoh's'. סָרִיס (from Akkadian *ša rēši*, 'the one of the [king's] head') means a court official / royal functionary, and by extension a castrated eunuch; the eunuch-sense is in tension with Potifar's having a wife (ch 39), so the WoH translation renders the ASV-baseline 'officer' (the court-official sense). See the central glossary entry `saris-court-official-eunuch-ambiguity`.

*Sar ha-tabbachim* — 'the captain of the guard'. Literally 'chief of the *tabbachim*' (slaughterers / cooks / butchers); the office is conventionally 'captain of the guard' (ASV, supported by the Nevuzaradan *rav-tabbachim* parallel, 2 Kgs 25; Jer 39-52), with NJPS preferring 'chief steward' and the literal sense yielding 'chief of the slaughterers / chief executioner' (cf. the Aramaic *tabbachayya*, Dan 2:14). The WoH translation keeps the ASV-baseline 'captain of the guard'; see the central glossary entry `sar-ha-tabbachim-captain-of-the-guard`.

*Par'oh* is rendered **'Pharaoh'**, following the established chapter-12 through chapter-20 convention (every prior occurrence renders 'Pharaoh', not the transliteration 'Par'oh'). The brief's proper-name list ('Par'oh') is noted, but the established 'Pharaoh' convention governs pending any corpus-wide retransliteration pass.
